content: Nitric oxide (NO) donors, including isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN), isosorbide dinitrate (ISDN), nitroglycerin, and sodium nitroprusside, have been studied for their role in cervical ripening and induction of labor during the third trimester. These agents were compared to placebo, vaginal prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), intracervical PGE2, vaginal misoprostol, and intracervical Foley catheter in a systematic review of 23 trials involving 4,777 women. The findings are as follows: 1. Nitric Oxide Donors vs. Placebo: There was no significant difference in the likelihood of achieving vaginal delivery within 24 hours (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.15; low-quality evidence). No significant difference was observed in uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate (FHR) changes (RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.62; low-quality evidence), cesarean section rates (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.11; moderate-quality evidence), or serious neonatal morbidity/perinatal death (RR 1.61, 95% CI 0.08 to 33.26; low-quality evidence). Women treated with NO donors were less likely to have an unfavorable cervix at 12 to 24 hours (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.90). Uterine hyperstimulation without FHR changes was less frequent in the NO donor group (RR 0.05, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.80). Side effects such as nausea, headache, and vomiting were more common in women receiving NO donors. 2. Nitric Oxide Donors vs. Vaginal Prostaglandins: There was no significant difference in uterine hyperstimulation with FHR changes (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.21) or cesarean section rates. Fewer women in the NO donor group failed to achieve vaginal delivery within 24 hours (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.86; one trial, 400 women). Serious neonatal morbidity and maternal morbidity were not reported. 3. Nitric Oxide Donors vs. Intracervical Prostaglandins: A reduction in the number of women failing to achieve vaginal delivery within 24 hours was observed with NO donors (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.86; one trial, 400 women). However, this result was based on limited data from an abstract, and further confirmation is needed. No significant differences were found in uterine hyperstimulation with FHR changes (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.74) or serious neonatal morbidity/perinatal death (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.74). Fewer women in the NO donor group underwent cesarean section compared to those receiving intracervical prostaglandins (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.90). Serious maternal morbidity or death was not reported. 4. Nitric Oxide Donors vs. Vaginal Misoprostol: NO donors were associated with a lower rate of uterine hyperstimulation with FHR changes (RR 0.07, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.37). Cesarean section rates were similar between groups (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.21). One study reported that women in the NO donor group were more likely to fail to deliver within 24 hours (RR 5.33, 95% CI 1.62 to 17.55). Secondary outcomes showed an increase in the proportion of women with an unchanged or unfavorable cervix (RR 3.43, 95% CI 2.07 to 5.66) and a higher need for oxytocin augmentation (RR 2.67, 95% CI 1.31 to 5.45). However, significant heterogeneity was noted in these findings. Uterine hyperstimulation without FHR changes, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, low Apgar scores at five minutes, and analgesia requirements were lower in the NO donor group. 5. Nitric Oxide Donors vs. Intracervical Foley Catheter: There was no significant difference in cesarean section rates (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.39 to 2.59; one trial, 80 women). No other primary outcomes were reported. One study involving 75 participants did not contribute data to the review. Conclusions: The available evidence suggests that nitric oxide donors may be effective in improving cervical favorability compared to placebo. However, their overall impact on key labor and delivery outcomes remains uncertain. Additional high-quality research is needed to better understand the role of NO donors in labor induction and to evaluate their safety and efficacy comprehensively.
